Apply Database Migrations Inside a Transaction That Is Rolled Back

Source: R/frs_migration_trial.R
frs_migration_trial.Rd

Applies one or more migration files to conn inside a single transaction, and registers the rollback to fire when env exits. The effect of a pending migration can then be measured, or tests run against it, without migrating a database other people use.

Usage

frs_migration_trial(conn, files, env = parent.frame())

Arguments

conn

A DBI::DBIConnection object. Must not already be in a transaction — DBI::dbBegin() errors on one that is.

files

Character. Paths to the migration files, applied in the order given. Every file is read and checked before the first one runs, so a refusal anywhere leaves the database untouched.

env

An environment. The rollback is deferred to its exit (withr::defer()), so it fires when the calling function returns. A refusal after file n has run is undone by that deferred rollback, not by the refusal itself. The global environment is refused: there its exit is the end of the session, so the trial would hold its transaction — and every lock the migration's DDL took — open and unannounced until R quits. Call it from inside a function, which is also what makes the rollback observable.

Value

The connection, invisibly.

Details

fwapg's migrations carry their own BEGIN; and COMMIT;. Left in, that COMMIT; would commit the trial's transaction, so the pair is stripped and any other transaction control is refused before anything runs. The backstop is that the session must still hold the transaction it opened, with the same id, after each file: a migration that committed and began again would hold another. That check detects a commit, after the fact — it cannot prevent one. Preventing is the screen's job, and the screen is what the files guarantee above is about.

What a rollback cannot undo is covered by neither check, so those calls are refused too: work committed on another connection (dblink, pg_background, a shell through COPY ... FROM PROGRAM), sequence changes (setval, nextval) and files written on the server (lo_export, pg_file_write). The scan reaches inside function bodies, because the migration may call what it creates.

Those are token refusals, not measurements of what a statement would do: a DEFAULT nextval('s') clause draws nothing at DDL time and is refused anyway, while a serial column — identical semantics — is not named and passes. The list errs toward refusing. Read a migration before trying it; a refusal is a reason to look, not proof of a hazard.

Transaction control is looked for only where the server would execute it: comments, string literals and dollar-quoted bodies are blanked first, with line breaks kept, so a plpgsql body's own BEGIN / END; / END IF; is not mistaken for the statement that would end the trial's transaction (fwapg's db/schema.sql writes bare END; seven times). A region that never closes — an unterminated comment, string or dollar quote — is a refusal rather than a guess, because the scan would otherwise be reading the wrong half of the file. COMMIT inside a body is left to the server, which answers invalid transaction termination while the trial holds an explicit transaction block.

See also

Other database: frs_db_conn(), frs_db_query()

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# measure a pending migration's effect, then let the rollback fire
measure <- function(migrations) {
  conn <- frs_db_conn()
  on.exit(DBI::dbDisconnect(conn), add = TRUE)
  frs_migration_trial(conn, migrations)
  DBI::dbGetQuery(conn, "SELECT count(*) FROM whse_basemapping.fwa_stream_networks_sp")
}
measure(c("~/Projects/repo/fwapg/db/migrations/202610131654__watershedatmeasure_drop_exbc.sql",
          "~/Projects/repo/fwapg/db/migrations/202610240132__indexpoint_tiebreak.sql"))
} # }
